metaTitle: Pallet Glossary: Pallet Terms A to Z — AGL Pallet
metaDescription: Plain definitions of pallet terms from A to Z: deckboards, stringers, blocks, notches, entry types, GMA, HT, MB, ISPM-15, load ratings, racking, and more.
intro: Definitions are written for buyers and are kept short. Where a term has a full guide, the definition links to it. Industry usage varies, so confirm any term that matters to an order in the written spec.

terms.definition: A solid or composite spacer, usually wood, that sits between the top and bottom decks of a block pallet in place of stringers. A 48 × 40 block pallet commonly uses nine blocks.
A pallet built on blocks rather than continuous stringers, giving true four-way entry for both forklifts and pallet jacks. Common in pooled and automated systems.
The boards on the underside of a pallet. A bottom deck spreads the load on conveyors, racking, and stacked pallets.
The ability of a pallet to carry a load across an unsupported span, such as between rack beams. Poor bridging shows up as deflection or sagging.
A large piece of lumber sawn on two or more sides that is later resawn into deckboards or stringers.
A bevel cut along the edge of a bottom deckboard, usually at the pallet's entry ends, that helps pallet jack wheels roll onto and off the bottom deck.
A pallet pooling company whose blue pallets are rented to shippers and returned through its network rather than sold. See pooled pallet.
A second stringer fastened alongside a damaged one as a repair. Its presence is one of the marks that separates Grade B from Grade A in common usage.
Lumber that has been sawn to the finished lengths, widths, and thicknesses a pallet design calls for, ready for assembly.
Any board that forms the top or bottom surface of a pallet. Deckboards run perpendicular to stringers on a stringer pallet.
The share of a deck's surface covered by boards rather than gaps. Higher coverage supports small cartons and bags better and adds weight and cost.
How far a pallet bends under load. Racked and free-span loads are usually limited by acceptable deflection, not just by breaking strength.
An ISPM-15 treatment that heats wood with microwave or radio-frequency energy. Marked DH on the treatment stamp.
A pallet with both a top and a bottom deck. If the decks match, it is reversible.
A pallet whose top and bottom deckboards both extend past the outer stringers. Used for sling and crane handling.
Loose wood or other material used to brace, block, or separate cargo in transit. Wood dunnage crossing a border falls under ISPM-15.
The load a pallet can carry while it is being moved by a forklift or pallet jack. Usually lower than the static rating.
The openings between decks where forklift tines or pallet jack forks go in. Pallets are described as two-way or four-way by how many sides allow entry.
A 1200 × 800 mm block pallet common in Europe, managed under the EPAL exchange system when marked accordingly.
The nails, staples, or screws that hold a pallet together. Fastener type, length, and pattern have a large effect on durability.
A pallet whose deckboards end flush with the outer stringers or blocks, with no overhang.
A pallet's length and width, stated with the stringer length first in North America, such as 48 × 40.
A pallet that allows entry from all four sides. See partial four-way and true four-way.
A pallet supported only at two edges, as on rack beams, with nothing under the middle. The most demanding way to support a loaded pallet.
The 48 × 40 inch stringer pallet footprint popularized by the Grocery Manufacturers Association for grocery and consumer-goods shipping.
A trade label, such as A, B, #1, or #2, describing a pallet's condition or lumber quality. Grade names are not a published standard.
Lumber that has not been dried and still holds a high moisture content. Common in pallet building; it shrinks and lightens as it dries.
A pallet roughly half a standard footprint, such as 48 × 20 or 24 × 40 in North America, used for store displays and smaller loads.
Lumber from broadleaf trees such as oak or poplar. In pallets, hardwood is common in the eastern United States and tends to be dense and heavy.
An ISPM-15 treatment in which the wood core reaches at least 56 °C (133 °F) for 30 continuous minutes. Marked HT on the treatment stamp.
The International Plant Protection Convention, the international treaty body that adopts ISPM-15 and owns the wheat-ear symbol used in treatment marks.
International Standard for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15, which sets treatment and marking rules for wood packaging in international trade.
The ISO standard listing principal dimensions for flat pallets used in intercontinental handling, including 1219 × 1016 mm (48 × 40 in).
Lumber dried in a kiln to a target moisture content. Kiln drying controls moisture; it is not the same as heat treatment for ISPM-15.
The weight a pallet can safely carry under stated support conditions: static, dynamic, or racked.
A fumigant approved under ISPM-15 but restricted in many countries because it depletes ozone. Marked MB on the treatment stamp.
The weight of water in wood as a percentage of its oven-dry weight. It affects pallet weight, shrinkage, fastener holding, and mold risk.
A cutout in the bottom of a stringer that lets forklift tines enter from the side, turning a two-way stringer pallet into a partial four-way pallet.
The government plant protection agency that enforces ISPM-15 in a country. In the United States it is USDA APHIS.
A pallet expected to make a single trip and not come back to the shipper. Often lighter and lower in cost than a multi-trip design.
Product or packaging that extends past the pallet's edge. Overhang weakens cartons and can cause damage in transit.
A notched stringer pallet: forklifts enter all four sides, but pallet jacks enter only the two unnotched ends.
A hand or powered truck with forks that slide under a pallet and lift it just off the floor. Its wheels need open bottom-deck space to enter.
Steel shelving systems that hold loaded pallets off the floor, usually on two beams. Racked pallets need a rating for the rack's support condition.
A molded pallet made from plastic resin. Exempt from ISPM-15 and often used in closed loops, food, and pharma.
A pallet rented from a pallet pool and returned through the pool's network rather than bought outright.
A molded pallet made from wood fibers and resin under heat and pressure. Processed wood, so exempt from ISPM-15, and often nestable.
The load a pallet can carry while supported on rack beams. Usually the lowest of the three ratings.
A pallet rebuilt from salvaged components. AGL sources new pallets only.
A double-face pallet whose top and bottom decks are identical, so either side can carry the load.
A platform with runners or stringers and no bottom deck. Often used for heavy machinery and loads that stay put.
Lumber from conifers such as Southern Yellow Pine or spruce. Lighter than most hardwoods and common in pooled and export pallets.
The load a pallet can carry sitting on a flat floor, not moving. Usually the highest of the three ratings.
A continuous board running the length of a pallet between the decks. A 48 × 40 stringer pallet usually has three.
A pallet built on stringers rather than blocks. The most common construction for one-way and domestic shipping in North America.
The load-carrying surface of a pallet. Top deckboard count and spacing set how well the deck supports cartons.
The bordered ISPM-15 mark showing the IPPC symbol, country code, facility number, and treatment code.
A pallet, usually block construction, that both forklifts and pallet jacks can enter from all four sides.
A pallet that allows entry from only two opposite sides, such as an unnotched stringer pallet.
Product, packaging, and pallet handled together as one piece. Pallet design is best judged as part of the whole unit load.
The portion of a deckboard that extends beyond the outer stringer. See double-wing pallet.
